screens.title: Data Replication and Failover/Failback
screens.narratorSegment: Today we'll build an intuitive picture of Snowflake data replication and failover groups. Replication creates continuously synchronized, read-only copies of a primary database in other accounts or regions so your data remains available even when the original account or region is unavailable. Failover groups take that replication scaffolding and add role management: they let you coordinate the promotion of a set of related objects so an entire application can switch to a different account as one unit. You'll see why this matters for disaster recovery, business continuity, and serving read workloads near users. We'll use the exact Snowflake commands the platform supports for creating replicas and promoting a replica to primary. A concrete example: creating a replica with CREATE DATABASE... AS REPLICA OF and later promoting a replica failover group with ALTER FAILOVER GROUP... PRIMARY. Common mistakes include assuming a replica is writable or skipping failover testing; we'll highlight both. By the end you'll understand what replication copies, what failover groups manage, and how to plan tests so failover succeeds when you need it most.

Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › Data Replication
Data Replication and Failover/Failback
Why it matters: keep data available across accounts and regions for DR, BC, and lower-latency reads.
In this lesson

You will learn how Snowflake copies a primary database to secondary accounts, how failover groups coordinate role changes across related objects, and the commands to create replicas and trigger failover.

Coming up

Examples include CREATE DATABASE ... AS REPLICA OF and ALTER FAILOVER GROUP ... PRIMARY, plus a simulated hands-on activity to practice failover and failback.

Key takeaway

Replication keeps synchronized copies; failover groups let you promote a replica to writable to resume operations.

Concept map

Writable source of truth. Origin for replication.
Replica(s)

Explore Key Topics
Database Replication
Continuous, incremental copies to target accounts and regions for availability and read locality.

Group related objects so they switch primary/secondary roles together during failover.

Plan, test, and monitor replication and failover to keep applications running.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your practice toward practical skills you can apply in Snowflake. First, you'll be able to explain what database replication is and why it supports disaster recovery and business continuity. That means describing continuous, incremental synchronization and how a secondary database differs from a primary. Second, you'll learn to differentiate database replication from failover groups. Replication copies data; failover groups coordinate which account acts as primary for a collection of objects. Third, you will configure a secondary database as a replica by using Snowflake commands like CREATE DATABASE... AS REPLICA OF and monitoring with SHOW REPLICATION DATABASES. Fourth, you will perform manual failover and failback by creating a failover group, creating its replica, and issuing ALTER FAILOVER GROUP... PRIMARY to promote a replica. Each skill matters: understanding the distinction prevents mistaken writes to replicas; testing failover avoids surprises. Practice these steps conceptually before running them in production to avoid accidental role changes.

screens.title: What is Database Replication in Snowflake?
screens.narratorSegment: Database replication in Snowflake is the process of copying a primary, writable database from a source account to one or more target accounts as secondary databases that are initially read-only. The key characteristics are continuous synchronization, incremental updates, and strong consistency so that replicas reflect changes from the primary over time. A concrete example from the chapter shows how, in a target account, the administrator runs CREATE DATABASE my_data_replica AS REPLICA OF. my_data to establish the replica. This is not a one-time dump; Snowflake keeps the replica updated efficiently. Why this matters: replicas let you serve read-heavy analytics near users in other regions and provide a pre-built copy for disaster recovery. A common misconception is to treat a replica as a writable backup. Initially, replicas are read-only and must be promoted via failover to become writable. Misunderstanding this can lead to failed writes and confusion during an incident. Takeaway: replication gives you synchronized read copies; treating replicas as writable without promotion is a critical mistake. Consider: how often will your workloads accept the inherent replication lag when planning RPOs? What is Database Replication in Snowflake? means a continuous, incremental copy of a primary database to target accounts so data remains available and can be promoted when needed.. In practical terms, definition, purpose, and the primary characteristics of replicas. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › What is Database Replication?
Definition
Continuous, incremental copying of a primary database to one or more secondary databases in target accounts or regions.
Why it matters
  • Enables disaster recovery and business continuity by providing available data copies.
  • Serves read-only analytics near users to reduce latency.
  • Facilitates account-to-account data migration without exporting external files.
Common misconception
Replicas are read-only by default; assuming they are writable without promotion leads to failed writes and operational confusion.
Concrete example
-- In the target account, as ACCOUNTADMIN
CREATE DATABASE my_data_replica AS REPLICA OF <source_account_name>.my_data;

-- Verify replication status
SHOW REPLICATION DATABASES;
This creates a read-only replica that Snowflake keeps synchronized.
Key takeaway

Use CREATE DATABASE ... AS REPLICA OF to establish a read-only copy; plan for replication lag and test read patterns against replicas.

screens.title: How Snowflake Synchronizes Replicas
screens.narratorSegment: Let's trace how Snowflake keeps a replica up to date. After you create a replica, Snowflake applies changes from the primary to the secondary in an incremental manner. This means only the deltas — new or changed micro-partitions and metadata — move across accounts, which optimizes bandwidth and latency. You can monitor replication using SHOW REPLICATION DATABASES to check status and lag indicators. A concrete example: create a table and insert rows on the primary, then run SELECT on the replica once synchronization completes to confirm the new rows are visible. One misconception to avoid is expecting zero lag: replication is efficient but not instantaneous, and your recovery point objective (RPO) should allow for short replication lag. Another operational nuance is that replicas are read-only until a failover event or promotion; attempting to write to a replica will fail. Takeaway: plan polling or checks in your runbook to verify replication status before initiating failover, and ask yourself where your acceptable lag boundary should be for your business needs. How Snowflake Synchronizes Replicas means snowflake sends incremental updates from primary to replica and exposes replication status so you can monitor health and lag.. In practical terms, continuous, incremental synchronization and monitoring. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › How Synchronization Works
Incremental flow
Changes on the primary are captured and transferred as deltas, updating replicas efficiently without full copies each time.
Monitoring
Use SHOW REPLICATION DATABASES to view replication status and identify lag. Schedule checks in your runbook to avoid promoting a stale replica.
Misconception
Expecting zero latency. Replication is fast and incremental, but lag exists and should inform your RPO.
Check your understanding
When would you accept a few minutes of lag to gain geographic read locality? When would you require near-zero lag for transactional workloads?
Example scenario
On the primary: INSERT rows into my_source_table. After replication and SHOW REPLICATION DATABASES shows the replica is current, SELECT from the replica to confirm visibility. Writes to the replica will fail until a failover promotes it.
Practical note
Include replication status checks in automation that triggers failover to ensure you promote an up-to-date replica.
Key takeaway

Replication is continuous and incremental; monitor status and plan for lag in your recovery objectives.

screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through the commands used in the target account to create and verify a replica. Conceptually, you create the replica as ACCOUNTADMIN in the target account with CREATE DATABASE my_replica_db AS REPLICA OF. my_source_db. After the replica exists, grant usage on database and schema and grant SELECT on tables so readers can query the replica. The chapter offers this concrete command sequence and the important verification step: use SHOW REPLICATION DATABASES and perform SELECT queries to confirm data presence. A common mistake is attempting INSERT into the replica before a failover; such writes will fail because the replica is read-only until promoted. Another operational point is to replace placeholder account identifiers with the real values for your accounts. Takeaway: follow the explicit create-verify-grant pattern and treat the replica as read-only until failover, and ask: who needs read access during normal operations and how will those roles change during failover? keyIdea.text: Run CREATE DATABASE ... AS REPLICA OF, grant usage and select, and verify with SHOW REPLICATION DATABASES and SELECT queries.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › Creating a Replica
Code walkthrough (target account)
-- In TARGET_ACCOUNT, as ACCOUNTADMIN
CREATE DATABASE my_replica_db AS REPLICA OF <source_account_identifier>.my_source_db;

-- Grant read access on the replica
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE my_replica_db TO ROLE PUBLIC;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA my_replica_db.public TO ROLE PUBLIC;
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE my_replica_db.public.my_source_table TO ROLE PUBLIC;

-- Verify the replica
USE DATABASE my_replica_db;
SELECT * FROM my_replica_db.public.my_source_table;
Note: attempts to INSERT will fail on a replica until the replica is promoted via failover.
Concrete tip
Replace placeholders with your actual account identifiers. Keep an inventory of allowed accounts for replication targets.
Misconception
Don't assume granted roles on the primary carry over automatically; explicitly grant usage and select on the replica as needed.
Key takeaway

Create the replica, grant minimal required privileges, and verify data with SELECT before relying on the replica for reads.

screens.title: Failover Groups — Purpose and Structure
screens.narratorSegment: A failover group is a Snowflake object used to coordinate failover and failback for a set of related objects, such as databases and shares. The failover group doesn't copy data by itself; it builds on database replication and manages role assignment — which account is primary and which is secondary — for a collection of objects that must transition together to preserve application consistency. The chapter's example shows creating a failover group with OBJECT_TYPES = DATABASES, SHARES and specifying which databases belong to the group and which accounts are allowed as targets. A concrete command is CREATE FAILOVER GROUP my_failover_group OBJECT_TYPES = DATABASES, SHARES ALLOWED_DATABASES = my_app_db, my_config_db ALLOWED_ACCOUNTS =. A common misunderstanding is treating a failover group as a backup mechanism that duplicates data; instead, it coordinates promotion and demotion across already-replicated objects. Takeaway: you use replication to copy data and failover groups to switch roles for entire application footprints so your app can resume operation in another account. Failover Groups — Purpose and Structure means a control object that coordinates primary/secondary roles for related replicated objects to preserve application consistency during failover.. In practical terms, why failover groups exist and what they control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › Failover Groups
Concept
Failover groups let you group databases and shares so they can be failed over together, ensuring an application's components move in lockstep during a role change.
Creation example
-- In the primary account, as ACCOUNTADMIN
CREATE FAILOVER GROUP my_failover_group
  OBJECT_TYPES = DATABASES, SHARES
  ALLOWED_DATABASES = my_app_db, my_config_db
  ALLOWED_ACCOUNTS = <target_account_name_1>, <target_account_name_2>;
This declares the set of objects and which accounts may act as targets for failover.
Why group objects?
Applications often depend on multiple databases or shares. Failing over only one database could leave dependent services inconsistent. A failover group preserves integrity by switching all members simultaneously.
Misconception
Failover groups do not replicate data. Data copying remains the job of database replication; failover groups manage which copy is primary.
Key takeaway

Use failover groups to coordinate role switching for related objects so an application can move to a new account without partial failures.

screens.title: Creating a Failover Group Replica
screens.narratorSegment: After you create a failover group in the primary account, you must create a replica of that group in each target account so the group can be promoted there. The chapter shows the specific S Q L you run in the target account as ACCOUNTADMIN: CREATE FAILOVER GROUP my_failover_group_replica AS REPLICA OF. my_failover_group; This command establishes the group replica and ties it to the source. Practically, you will also ensure that each database included in the group has been replicated and that privileges are correctly granted in the target account so that, if promoted, ownership and roles work as expected. A common mistake is creating a failover group replica before its member databases are replicated or without confirming required grants; this can lead to promotion failures or permission errors during failover. Takeaway: create the group replica only after member databases exist as replicas and verify ownership and grants in the target account. content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › Failover Group Replica
Command example
-- In a TARGET_ACCOUNT, as ACCOUNTADMIN
CREATE FAILOVER GROUP my_failover_group_replica AS REPLICA OF <source_account_name>.my_failover_group;
Before running this, ensure each database included in the group already exists as a replica in the target account and required grants exist so ownership and access will be valid after promotion.
Common mistake
Creating the failover group replica before its member databases are available or without verifying grants. This can prevent promotion or cause permission issues during failover.
Verification steps
  • Confirm replicas exist with SHOW REPLICATION DATABASES.
  • Check grants and ownership in target account.
  • Ensure allowed accounts are correct in the primary group's definition.
Key takeaway

Create the failover group replica only after verifying its member databases are replicated and privileges are set, so promotions succeed when needed.

screens.title: Performing a Failover
screens.narratorSegment: A failover operation promotes a secondary failover group in a target account to become the new primary. You run ALTER FAILOVER GROUP my_failover_group_replica PRIMARY in the target account to trigger this. As a result, the databases within that group become writable in the new primary account and the original primary's databases become read-only. This switch allows applications to connect to a different account and resume operations, but expect a brief downtime while connection strings and permissions stabilize. A concrete example in the chapter shows running ALTER FAILOVER GROUP my_app_fg_replica PRIMARY, then using USE DATABASE and performing an INSERT to confirm the promoted database is writable. A common misconception is assuming failover automatically updates application connections; in practice you must plan connection changes, DNS updates, or service redirects as part of the failover runbook. Takeaway: failover promotes writability in the new account but requires planned application cutover steps — ask what your application needs to reconnect successfully after promotion. screens.title: Replica vs Primary — Behavior and Permissions
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the practical differences between a primary database and its replicas helps avoid operational mistakes. The primary database is writable, accepts DML and DDL changes, and is the authoritative source for replication. Secondary databases are read-only copies that Snowflake keeps synchronized; they cannot accept writes until they are promoted via failover. A concrete scenario: insert a row into the primary, and after synchronization you will see that row on the replica via SELECT. Attempting to INSERT directly into the replica will fail. Permission handling differs too: you must grant usage and SELECT privileges explicitly on replicas as needed. A common misunderstanding is assuming privileges and ownership map identically between primary and replica without checking. Takeaway: treat replicas as read-only query endpoints until you intentionally promote them. Reflect: which jobs in your environment should run only on replicas, and which must remain on the primary? screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough follows the chapter's hands-on activity in a conceptual lab with two accounts: SOURCE_ACCOUNT and TARGET_ACCOUNT. keyIdea.text: Create a source DB and enable replication, create the replica and grant access, create the failover group and its replica, then promote the replica to simulate failover.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › Hands-on Simulation
SOURCE_ACCOUNT (conceptual)
-- In SOURCE_ACCOUNT, as ACCOUNTADMIN
CREATE DATABASE my_source_db;
USE DATABASE my_source_db;
CREATE SCHEMA public;
CREATE TABLE my_source_table (id INT, name VARCHAR);
INSERT INTO my_source_table VALUES (1, 'Alice'), (2, 'Bob');

ALTER DATABASE my_source_db ENABLE REPLICATION TO ACCOUNTS <target_account_identifier>;
Enable replication so the target can create a replica.
TARGET_ACCOUNT (conceptual)
-- In TARGET_ACCOUNT, as ACCOUNTADMIN
CREATE DATABASE my_replica_db AS REPLICA OF <source_account_identifier>.my_source_db;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE my_replica_db TO ROLE PUBLIC;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA my_replica_db.public TO ROLE PUBLIC;
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE my_replica_db.public.my_source_table TO ROLE PUBLIC;

-- Create failover group replica
CREATE FAILOVER GROUP my_app_fg_replica AS REPLICA OF <source_account_identifier>.my_app_fg;

-- Simulate failover
ALTER FAILOVER GROUP my_app_fg_replica PRIMARY;
USE DATABASE my_source_db;
INSERT INTO my_source_db.public.my_source_table VALUES (3, 'Charlie');
Verify that inserts are accepted after promotion and that the original source becomes read-only.
Key takeaway

Follow the create-replicate-grant-verify-promote sequence and always practice in non-production before executing in live systems.

fullNarratorScript:
Today we'll build an intuitive picture of Snowflake data replication and failover groups. Replication creates continuously synchronized, read-only copies of a primary database in other accounts or regions so your data remains available even when the original account or region is unavailable. Failover groups take that replication scaffolding and add role management: they let you coordinate the promotion of a set of related objects so an entire application can switch to a different account as one unit. You'll see why this matters for disaster recovery, business continuity, and serving read workloads near users. We'll use the exact Snowflake commands the platform supports for creating replicas and promoting a replica to primary. A concrete example: creating a replica with CREATE DATABASE... AS REPLICA OF and later promoting a replica failover group with ALTER FAILOVER GROUP... PRIMARY. Common mistakes include assuming a replica is writable or skipping failover testing; we'll highlight both. By the end you'll understand what replication copies, what failover groups manage, and how to plan tests so failover succeeds when you need it most.

These objectives focus your practice toward practical skills you can apply in Snowflake. First, you'll be able to explain what database replication is and why it supports disaster recovery and business continuity. That means describing continuous, incremental synchronization and how a secondary database differs from a primary. Second, you'll learn to differentiate database replication from failover groups. Replication copies data; failover groups coordinate which account acts as primary for a collection of objects. Third, you will configure a secondary database as a replica by using Snowflake commands like CREATE DATABASE... AS REPLICA OF and monitoring with SHOW REPLICATION DATABASES. Fourth, you will perform manual failover and failback by creating a failover group, creating its replica, and issuing ALTER FAILOVER GROUP... PRIMARY to promote a replica. Each skill matters: understanding the distinction prevents mistaken writes to replicas; testing failover avoids surprises. Practice these steps conceptually before running them in production to avoid accidental role changes.

These additional objectives put replication and failover into practice. You will identify common use cases like disaster recovery, business continuity, global data distribution, and migration so you choose the right pattern. You will also learn to monitor replication status with SHOW REPLICATION DATABASES and to recognize replication lag as a factor when planning RPOs. A critical skill is testing: perform failover and failback in a non-production environment to verify connection changes, write promotion, and data synchronization. Finally, you'll learn best practices: grant minimal privileges on replicas, plan for application connection string changes during failover, and schedule regular DR drills. Each description maps back to commands and the hands-on simulation in the chapter. Practicing these behaviors prevents the common mistake of assuming replication alone is a complete DR solution and helps you design repeatable, safe failover procedures.

Database replication in Snowflake is the process of copying a primary, writable database from a source account to one or more target accounts as secondary databases that are initially read-only. The key characteristics are continuous synchronization, incremental updates, and strong consistency so that replicas reflect changes from the primary over time. A concrete example from the chapter shows how, in a target account, the administrator runs CREATE DATABASE my_data_replica AS REPLICA OF. my_data to establish the replica. This is not a one-time dump; Snowflake keeps the replica updated efficiently. Why this matters: replicas let you serve read-heavy analytics near users in other regions and provide a pre-built copy for disaster recovery. A common misconception is to treat a replica as a writable backup. Initially, replicas are read-only and must be promoted via failover to become writable. Misunderstanding this can lead to failed writes and confusion during an incident. Takeaway: replication gives you synchronized read copies; treating replicas as writable without promotion is a critical mistake. Understanding the practical differences between a primary database and its replicas helps avoid operational mistakes. The primary database is writable, accepts DML and DDL changes, and is the authoritative source for replication. Secondary databases are read-only copies that Snowflake keeps synchronized; they cannot accept writes until they are promoted via failover. A concrete scenario: insert a row into the primary, and after synchronization you will see that row on the replica via SELECT. Attempting to INSERT directly into the replica will fail. Permission handling differs too: you must grant usage and SELECT privileges explicitly on replicas as needed. A common misunderstanding is assuming privileges and ownership map identically between primary and replica without checking. Takeaway: treat replicas as read-only query endpoints until you intentionally promote them. Reflect: which jobs in your environment should run only on replicas, and which must remain on the primary?
